limitations: Few studies have taken a fully robust, empirical approach, often being purely descriptive or testing questions 'in the lab' outside of actual building contexts (p. 11).
Statistics are often descriptive (e.g., reporting means) rather than comparing groups, making cross-study comparisons difficult (p. 11).
Few studies have approached research in biophilic architecture with an embodied cognition framework (p. 11).
Few studies measure physiological responses (e.g., skin conductivity, brain region activation) (p. 11).
Many studies observe human responses to naturalness in natural landscapes or solely organic natural forms, or use images instead of actual environmental experience (p. 11).

Many inferences must be made, such as applying findings on natural or computer-generated fractals to architectural fractals, or using greenspace data to infer effects of imitations of natural forms (p. 12).
Virtual reality (VR) and fMRI studies, while useful for subcortical regions, may not be as ecologically valid as testing differences in actual buildings (p. 12).
minimum_safe_summary: This paper reviews existing neuroscientific, architectural, and psychological research on biophilic architecture's impact on well-being, and includes an empirical re-analysis of publicly available data. The core claim is that biophilic architecture, by connecting users with nature through natural elements and forms, can significantly improve human well-being, health, and mood. Key findings from the re-analysis show that natural environments (greenspaces) increase positive affect, reduce stressful thought, and promote spontaneous thought compared to urban environments. The review also highlights that fractal patterns (D values 1.3-1.5) reduce physiological stress, high ceilings boost creativity and comfort, and natural light reduces depression and improves sleep quality. Limitations include a lack of robust empirical studies in real-world settings, reliance on descriptive statistics, limited use of embodied cognition frameworks, and insufficient measurement of physiological responses or neural activity in architectural contexts.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Biophilic architecture: Using cognitive science principles to understand impact on well-being
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Biophilic architecture is an approach that seeks to connect users more closely with nature by utilizing natural elements and landscape features in buildings. Its aim is to increase well-being, health, and mood using the built environment that surrounds us. Similarly, and often used in tandem, biomorphic architecture refers to an approach that seeks to connect users more closely with nature by using features that mimic it. Despite these goals, little research in cognitive science, the study of the mind, has explored the underlying cognitive reactions specifically induced by biophilic architecture. Here, I have compiled neuroscientific, architectural, and psychological research to study the effects of biophilic architecture on mood, stress, and general health outcomes, and suggest further areas of study for future research. Early findings suggest green spaces and biophilic architecture are extremely effective in lowering stress, increasing happiness, and improving overall physiological health.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature, and biophilic architecture leverages this tendency to enhance well-being by satisfying fundamental human needs for nature.

Biophilic architectural elements (e.g., views of nature, natural patterns) facilitate 'soft fascination' and a sense of 'being away', leading to the restoration of directed attention and reduced mental fatigue.

Exposure to natural elements and views in biophilic architecture elicits immediate physiological and psychological stress reduction responses, such as decreased heart rate, lower blood pressure, and positive emotional states.

mechanism_chain.description: Biophilic architecture elements trigger cognitive and affective processes that lead to improved well-being outcomes by leveraging innate human responses to nature.
